name: Objective, Role, Action, Context, Layout/Length, Example
tagline: A well-rounded, six-part structure for everyday prompts.
whenToUse: ORACLE is the default choice when you're not sure which framework to reach for. It covers the six things almost any prompt benefits from: what you want, who the AI should act as, what to actually do, the background it needs, how the output should be shaped, and a concrete example. Use it for blog intros, emails, explainers, summaries, and general writing or research tasks.

components.name: Objective
components.description: The end result you're after — the single sentence that describes success.

components.name: Role
components.description: The persona or expertise you want the AI to adopt while answering.

components.name: Action
components.description: The specific task the AI needs to perform, stated as a clear instruction.

components.name: Context
components.description: Background details, audience, or constraints the AI needs to get it right.

components.name: Layout/Length
components.description: The format, structure, and rough length of the output.

components.name: Example
components.description: A sample of the tone, style, or structure you want it to match.

goodPrompt:
Objective: Get more small business owners to open our weekly newsletter.
Role: You are an email marketing strategist with experience writing for busy small business owners.
Action: Write three subject line options for our weekly newsletter.
Context: The newsletter covers one practical marketing tip per week. Our audience is time-poor and skeptical of hype.
Layout/Length: Three subject lines, each under 60 characters, no emojis.
Example: Similar in tone to "The 10-minute fix for your slowest page" — specific and low-hype.
exampleOutput: Three subject lines matching the brief, each specific rather than generic, each under the character limit, with a short one-line note on why each one works for a skeptical, time-poor reader.
supportedModels: ORACLE's plain, labeled-section format works well across ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini — it doesn't rely on any model-specific syntax, which is why PromptGeneratorLab uses it as the default framework.

name: Role, Action, Context, Example
tagline: A fast, four-part structure for when you need a good prompt in under a minute.
whenToUse: RACE strips ORACLE down to the essentials. Reach for it when the task is simple enough that you don't need to spell out layout and length separately — quick drafts, short-form content, one-off questions, and situations where you'd rather move fast than be exhaustive.

components.name: Role
components.description: Who the AI should be while it answers — this shapes vocabulary and judgment more than any other single instruction.

components.name: Action
components.description: The exact thing you want done, phrased as a direct instruction rather than a vague ask.

components.name: Context
components.description: Just enough background for the answer to be usable — audience, purpose, or constraints.

components.name: Example
components.description: A short reference point so the AI can match your intended tone or format.

goodPrompt:
Role: You are a social media manager for a bootstrapped SaaS product.
Action: Write five tweet ideas announcing a new feature.
Context: The feature is a dark mode toggle. Our audience is mostly developers who dislike marketing-speak.
Example: Tone should be closer to a changelog entry than an ad — plain, specific, a little dry.
exampleOutput: Five short tweet drafts, each announcing the feature from a slightly different angle (the feature itself, why it exists, a specific use case, a light joke, a direct CTA), written in the plain, low-hype tone the example called for.
supportedModels: RACE works well as a universal format, and is especially effective with ChatGPT and Claude for short-form, high-frequency content where speed matters more than exhaustive detail.

name: Context, Action, Result, Example
tagline: A result-oriented structure that keeps the AI focused on the outcome you actually need.
whenToUse: CARE is useful whenever the deliverable matters more than the process — reports, summaries, business writing, and any task where you want the AI to work backward from a defined result instead of just following instructions step by step.

components.name: Context
components.description: The situation the AI is operating in — what's happening and why this task exists.

components.name: Action
components.description: What you need the AI to do to move from the current situation toward the result.

components.name: Result
components.description: The specific outcome that defines a successful answer — what "done" looks like.

components.name: Example
components.description: A model of the format, tone, or level of detail the result should have.

goodPrompt:
Context: Our Q3 sales data shows growth in two regions and a decline in one, and leadership has 10 minutes before a board meeting.
Action: Summarize the data into the key takeaways leadership needs to know.
Result: A summary that lets a non-analyst understand what changed and why, without needing to read the underlying spreadsheet.
Example: Similar structure to a three-bullet executive summary — headline number, driver, one recommended action.
exampleOutput: A short executive summary with a headline figure, the main driver behind the regional decline, and one recommended next step — formatted for someone reading it in the elevator before a meeting, not an analyst.
supportedModels: CARE is a strong fit for both ChatGPT and Claude when the task is business or analytical writing, since naming the Result up front keeps longer-context models from wandering into unnecessary detail.

name: Action, Purpose, Expectation
tagline: The shortest useful framework — three parts, built for speed.
whenToUse: APE is the framework to reach for when you need something quick and the task is genuinely simple: a rewrite, a short explanation, a single piece of copy. It trades thoroughness for speed, so it's not the right choice for anything with real nuance or multiple constraints.

components.name: Action
components.description: The task itself, stated plainly.

components.name: Purpose
components.description: Why you need it — this single line of "why" often does more to improve output than extra instructions would.

components.name: Expectation
components.description: What the finished output should look or feel like.

badPrompt: Rewrite this sentence to sound better.
goodPrompt:
Action: Rewrite this sentence: "Our product helps you manage tasks more efficiently."
Purpose: It's the first line of our homepage and needs to earn a second sentence of attention.
Expectation: One sentence, more specific and concrete than the original, no buzzwords like "efficiently" or "seamless."
exampleOutput: A single rewritten sentence that replaces the vague claim with something concrete and specific to what the product actually does, matching the length and tone constraint given.
supportedModels: APE's brevity makes it a good match for quick ChatGPT sessions and for Claude when you want a fast, low-friction first draft to iterate on.

name: Characterise, Request, Examples, Adjust, Test, Evaluate
tagline: A six-part, iteration-friendly framework built for getting the details right.
whenToUse: CREATE is designed for tasks you expect to refine rather than get right on the first try — long-form content, technical writing, anything where the first draft is a starting point. It builds revision into the framework itself instead of treating it as an afterthought.

components.name: Characterise
components.description: Define the role, tone, and expertise the AI should bring to the task.

components.name: Request
components.description: State the core task clearly and specifically.

components.name: Examples
components.description: Show the style, structure, or reference material to draw from.

components.name: Adjust
components.description: Note any constraints or tweaks to apply on top of the base request.

components.name: Test
components.description: Describe how the output should be checked or validated before it's considered finished.

components.name: Evaluate
components.description: State the criteria that make the final output good enough to ship.

badPrompt: Write a technical guide about API rate limiting.
goodPrompt:
Characterise: You are a backend engineer writing documentation for other engineers.
Request: Write a guide explaining how to implement API rate limiting.
Examples: Follow the structure of Stripe's API docs — short paragraphs, code snippets, no marketing language.
Adjust: Focus on token bucket and sliding window approaches only; skip anything cloud-provider-specific.
Test: A mid-level backend engineer should be able to implement a basic version after reading it once.
Evaluate: Success means the guide has runnable code, not just conceptual explanation.
exampleOutput: A structured technical guide covering token bucket and sliding window rate limiting, with short explanatory paragraphs and runnable code examples in the style of vendor API documentation, avoiding marketing language.
supportedModels: CREATE's structure is particularly effective with Claude for longer technical or educational content, and works well with ChatGPT when you plan to iterate across multiple turns.

name: Task, Action, Goal
tagline: The simplest framework — three words, one clear instruction.
whenToUse: TAG is for genuinely small tasks where anything more elaborate would be overkill: a single email, a short list, a quick calculation, a one-off question. If you find yourself wanting to add a fourth section, the task probably needs RACE or ORACLE instead.

components.name: Task
components.description: What needs to get done, named directly.

components.name: Action
components.description: The specific step or output you want, not just the topic.

components.name: Goal
components.description: What success looks like for this specific task.

badPrompt: Help me with my to-do list.
goodPrompt:
Task: Organize my to-do list for tomorrow.
Action: Group these 8 items into "must do," "should do," and "if time allows."
Goal: I want to walk into tomorrow knowing exactly what the top 3 priorities are.
exampleOutput: The eight items sorted into the three named buckets, with the top three must-do items called out explicitly at the top so the priority is unambiguous at a glance.
supportedModels: TAG works equally well across ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini — its brevity means there's little room for model-specific phrasing to matter.

name: Context, Role, Evidence, Output
tagline: A framework built for answers that need to be grounded in specific evidence.
whenToUse: CREO is the right choice when you're asking the AI to reason from specific facts, data, or source material rather than general knowledge — research summaries, analysis of a document you're pasting in, or any task where you want the answer traceable back to what you gave it.

components.name: Context
components.description: The situation and what the evidence is being used to decide or explain.

components.name: Role
components.description: The expertise or perspective the AI should apply when interpreting the evidence.

components.name: Evidence
components.description: The specific facts, data, or material the answer must be grounded in.

components.name: Output
components.description: The exact form the answer should take.

badPrompt: What do you think about our survey results?
goodPrompt:
Context: We're deciding whether to prioritize a mobile app or a browser extension next quarter.
Role: You are a product strategist evaluating user research.
Evidence: 68% of respondents said they use our product primarily on desktop; 22% asked for mobile access; 10% mentioned browser workflow friction.
Output: A one-paragraph recommendation citing which numbers drove the conclusion.
exampleOutput: A one-paragraph recommendation that names a clear priority, explicitly ties the conclusion back to the specific percentages given rather than general assumptions about mobile usage.
supportedModels: CREO is especially strong with Claude for long-context, evidence-grounded analysis, and works well with ChatGPT when the evidence is pasted directly into the same conversation.

name: Role, Input, Steps, Expectation
tagline: A process-oriented framework for tasks that need to happen in a specific order.
whenToUse: RISE is built for multi-step tasks — anything where the AI needs to work through a sequence rather than produce one answer in a single pass. Use it for plans, procedures, tutorials, or any task where getting the order right matters as much as the content.

components.name: Role
components.description: The expertise the AI should bring to sequencing and executing the task.

components.name: Input
components.description: The starting material or situation the AI is working from.

components.name: Steps
components.description: The stages you want the AI to work through, in order.

components.name: Expectation
components.description: What the finished, step-by-step output should look like.

badPrompt: Help me plan a product launch.
goodPrompt:
Role: You are a product marketing manager who has run B2B SaaS launches before.
Input: We're launching a new analytics dashboard feature in 6 weeks, team of 4, modest budget.
Steps: Work through pre-launch (weeks 1-3), launch week, and post-launch (weeks 5-6) separately.
Expectation: A week-by-week checklist, not a narrative — something I can hand straight to the team.
exampleOutput: A week-by-week checklist broken into the three named phases, each with concrete action items sized for a 4-person team on a modest budget, formatted for direct handoff rather than prose.
supportedModels: RISE performs well with both ChatGPT and Claude for planning tasks, and is particularly effective with Claude when the plan needs to stay coherent across a long, detailed output.

name: Problem, Action, Information, Next Steps
tagline: A troubleshooting-focused framework for when something is broken and you need a fix.
whenToUse: PAIN is built for diagnostic and troubleshooting tasks — debugging, fixing a broken process, or working through any problem where you need the AI to reason from symptom to cause to fix, rather than just generate content.

components.name: Problem
components.description: What's actually going wrong, described as specifically as possible.

components.name: Action
components.description: What you want the AI to do about it — diagnose, fix, or explain.

components.name: Information
components.description: The relevant details: error messages, what you've already tried, environment specifics.

components.name: Next Steps
components.description: The form you want the resolution in — a fix, a checklist, a set of things to try.

badPrompt: My code isn't working, can you fix it?
goodPrompt:
Problem: My Node.js API returns a 500 error only when the request body is larger than ~1MB.
Action: Diagnose the likely cause and suggest a fix.
Information: Using Express 4.19, no custom body-parser limits set, error only appears in production, not locally.
Next Steps: Give me the specific config change to make, not a general explanation of body size limits.
exampleOutput: A diagnosis pointing to the default body-parser size limit as the likely cause, followed by the specific Express configuration change needed to raise it, rather than a general essay about payload limits.
supportedModels: PAIN works well with both ChatGPT and Claude for debugging tasks, and benefits from Claude's ability to hold a lot of surrounding code or log context when diagnosing less obvious bugs.

name: Context, Objective, Actions, Scenario, Task
tagline: A five-part framework for detailed, multi-constraint tasks.
whenToUse: COAST is worth the extra structure when a task has several moving parts that all need to be specified — detailed business writing, planning documents, or anything where leaving out one piece of context would meaningfully change the output.

components.name: Context
components.description: The background situation the task exists within.

components.name: Objective
components.description: What you're trying to achieve overall.

components.name: Actions
components.description: The specific things the AI needs to do to get there.

components.name: Scenario
components.description: The concrete situation or constraints the actions need to account for.

components.name: Task
components.description: The precise deliverable you want at the end.

badPrompt: Write a business plan for my idea.
goodPrompt:
Context: I'm starting a subscription coffee roasting business, solo founder, no funding yet.
Objective: I need a plan that helps me decide if this is worth pursuing before I invest more time.
Actions: Estimate startup costs, identify the biggest risk, and outline a lean first 90 days.
Scenario: I can work on this part-time for now and have about $5,000 to start.
Task: A one-page lean plan, not a full formal business plan document.
exampleOutput: A one-page lean plan covering rough startup costs within the stated budget, the single biggest risk to the idea, and a 90-day outline sized for part-time effort — not a formal multi-section business plan.
supportedModels: COAST is a good fit for both ChatGPT and Claude on detailed planning tasks, and its explicit Scenario section helps keep longer Claude outputs grounded in real constraints instead of generic advice.

name: Role, Objective, Scenario, Expected Solution, Steps
tagline: A structured, solution-oriented framework for consulting-style problems.
whenToUse: ROSES is suited to problems that need a considered recommendation rather than a straightforward answer — strategic decisions, tradeoff analysis, or anything where you want the AI to reason like a consultant working through a specific scenario toward a defined kind of solution.

components.name: Role
components.description: The expertise or perspective the AI should reason from.

components.name: Objective
components.description: The underlying goal behind the request.

components.name: Scenario
components.description: The specific situation, including relevant constraints and stakeholders.

components.name: Expected Solution
components.description: The type of answer you're looking for — a recommendation, a comparison, a decision.

components.name: Steps
components.description: How you want the reasoning or the answer broken down.

goodPrompt:
Role: You are a pricing strategist for small subscription businesses.
Objective: I want to increase revenue without losing too many existing customers.
Scenario: I run a $15/month tool with 400 subscribers, churn is currently 5% monthly, no price increase in 2 years.
Expected Solution: A specific recommendation, not a list of general pricing strategies.
Steps: State the recommendation first, then the reasoning, then one risk to watch for.
exampleOutput: A specific price-increase recommendation stated up front, followed by the reasoning tied to the given churn rate and subscriber count, and a named risk to monitor — not a generic list of pricing tactics.
supportedModels: ROSES works well with Claude for nuanced, tradeoff-heavy business reasoning, and with ChatGPT when you want a faster, more direct recommendation.

name: Review, Evaluate, Suggest, Enhance, Explain
tagline: A framework built specifically for improving something you've already written.
whenToUse: RESEE is different from the others: it's not for generating new content, it's for reviewing and refining content you already have. Use it for editing drafts, critiquing your own writing, or getting a second opinion on something before you publish or send it.

components.name: Review
components.description: Ask the AI to read the existing content carefully before responding.

components.name: Evaluate
components.description: Specify what to judge it against — clarity, tone, persuasiveness, accuracy.

components.name: Suggest
components.description: Ask for specific, actionable suggestions rather than vague feedback.

components.name: Enhance
components.description: Ask for an improved version, not just a critique.

components.name: Explain
components.description: Ask the AI to explain why each change helps, so you can apply the lesson elsewhere.

goodPrompt:
Review: Here is my email to a client about a missed deadline: [paste email].
Evaluate: Judge it on whether it sounds accountable without being overly apologetic.
Suggest: Point out any lines that sound defensive or overly formal.
Enhance: Rewrite it applying your suggestions.
Explain: Briefly explain the two biggest changes you made and why.
exampleOutput: Specific feedback identifying which lines read as defensive or overly formal, a rewritten version of the email, and a short explanation of the two most impactful changes so the pattern can be reused next time.
supportedModels: RESEE is especially effective with Claude for longer documents where nuanced tone feedback matters, and works well with ChatGPT for shorter, quicker edits.
